shareValue: A survival test for deciding which feature deserves to remain.
problemStatement: A technically working health tracker still failed to solve the decision its creator repeatedly faced.
solutionStatement: Remove the unused feature set and keep the small food-decision loop that gets used in real life.
caption:
Five months building a health tracker I never opened once.

The product problem was never "can I store more health data?" It was "can I make one small decision easier when I'm tired, hungry, and not thinking clearly?"

The only part I actually used was the wheel near the bottom that picked where to eat, so I deleted the rest. That was the builder's journey here: a lot of work, a narrower product, and a sharper answer to a real problem.

#buildinpublic #indiedev #iosdev #swiftui

slides.text: Five months of work survived as one tiny button.
It started as a health tracker.
Everything worked—but I never reached for it.
slides.kicker: The bug was product fit, not code quality.

slides.text: So I asked a more uncomfortable question.
slides.kicker: What decision am I trying to make faster?

slides.text: Keep the loop that gets used
items: Make the decision and move on

slides.text: The feature you actually use is the product.
slides.kicker: Everything else was support work. Useful, maybe. But not the reason the app existed.

items: Which feature gets used without reminders?
Which one solves a frequent decision?
What would nobody miss if it vanished?

captions.instagram:
Five months of code. One feature survived.

The health tracker worked—but I never reached for it. The food decision wheel was different: it solved a small, frequent problem when I was tired and hungry.

So the big app became the tiny feature. Usage made the decision clearer than pride ever could. Keep the survival test for the next time your roadmap feels crowded.

Which feature would your users miss if everything else disappeared?
